misconceptions.name: Letter as object (label)
misconceptions.description: A letter is read as a label for an object (apples, pears) instead of a number.
misconceptions.example: Anna buys a apples at 5 cents each and p pears at 3 cents each. What does the expression 5a + 3p give?
misconceptions.why: The letters are read as names of objects and the numbers as amounts of them.

misconceptions.name: Different letters must differ in value
misconceptions.description: Different letters are assumed to stand for different numbers.
misconceptions.example: Can c + d = 10 be true when c and d have the same value?
misconceptions.typical_wrong: No, different letters must stand for different numbers.
misconceptions.why: A letter is treated as a fixed name for one number, so two letters cannot share a value.

misconceptions.name: Value from alphabet position
misconceptions.description: The value of a letter is assumed from its place in the alphabet.
misconceptions.example: n + 5 = 12. What is n?
misconceptions.typical_wrong: n = 14, because n is the 14th letter.
misconceptions.why: The letter is evaluated by position, not solved for.

misconceptions.name: Conjoining terms
misconceptions.description: Terms are joined into a single term to 'finish' the expression.
misconceptions.example: Simplify 3x + 8.
misconceptions.why: The '+' is read as a request to produce one answer, so numbers and letter terms are combined.

misconceptions.name: Juxtaposition read as place value
misconceptions.description: In 2a the letter and number are read like digits in a numeral.
misconceptions.example: If a = 5, what is the value of 2a?
misconceptions.why: Analogy with place-value notation, where 25 means 2 tens and 5 ones.

misconceptions.name: Operational reading of '='
misconceptions.description: '=' is read as 'the answer comes next' rather than 'both sides have the same value'.
misconceptions.example: Fill in the box: 8 + 4 = □ + 5
misconceptions.why: The student adds the numbers on the left and writes the result, ignoring the right side.

misconceptions.name: Sign errors and one-sided operations
misconceptions.description: Terms are moved without changing sign, or an operation is applied to only one side.
misconceptions.example: Solve 3x + 5 = 20.
misconceptions.why: 'Moving' 5 across the equal sign without inverting the operation.

misconceptions.name: Distributive law applied to one term
misconceptions.description: A multiplier is applied to the first term in a bracket only ('linear extrapolation').
misconceptions.example: Expand 2(x + 3).
misconceptions.why: A valid rule is extended to a new situation but applied partially.

misconceptions.name: Square of a sum
misconceptions.description: The power is distributed over addition.
misconceptions.example: Expand (a + b)².
misconceptions.why: Distribution of the exponent over a sum, by analogy with (ab)² = a²b².

misconceptions.name: Reversal error
misconceptions.description: The letters follow the order of words in the sentence.
misconceptions.example: There are 6 times as many students (S) as professors (P). Which equation is correct?
misconceptions.why: Word order is mapped directly to symbol order ('6 S ... P').

misconceptions.topic: Negative numbers and the minus sign
misconceptions.name: Minus sign not distributed
misconceptions.description: The minus sign before a bracket is applied to the first term only.
misconceptions.example: Simplify −(x − 3).
misconceptions.why: The minus is read as belonging to x, not to the whole bracket.

misconceptions.topic: Negative numbers and the minus sign
misconceptions.name: Subtraction of a negative number
misconceptions.description: Natural-number rules about subtraction are carried over to negatives.
misconceptions.example: Calculate 5 − (−2).
misconceptions.why: 'Subtracting makes smaller' is applied without regard to the sign of the subtrahend.

misconceptions.name: Equal sign must come at the end
misconceptions.description: An equation is only accepted in the form "operation = answer".
misconceptions.example: True or false: 8 = 5 + 3?
misconceptions.typical_wrong: False, the answer must come after the equal sign.
misconceptions.why: "=" is read as "the answer comes next", so an operation on the right side looks wrong.

misconceptions.name: Negative base and square: -3² read as 9
Inequality sign not reversed when multiplying or dividing by a negative number
Pythagorean theorem assumed to hold for every triangle
misconceptions.typical_wrong: applies a² + b² = c² to a triangle without a right angle
misconceptions.correct: only right triangles; the converse is a test for a right angle

misconceptions.name: Sine read as a length; adjacent and opposite leg mixed up
misconceptions.typical_wrong: sin α = adjacent / hypotenuse, or sin α given in cm
misconceptions.correct: sin α = opposite / hypotenuse, a dimensionless ratio

misconceptions.name: Mean taken as the "typical value"; median read from unsorted data
misconceptions.typical_wrong: median of 7, 2, 9, 4, 5 is 9 (middle of the list as written)
misconceptions.correct: sort first: 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, so the median is 5

misconceptions.name: Slope and intercept confused; steeper line means larger y
Graph as picture
misconceptions.description: A graph is read as a picture of the situation.
misconceptions.example: A cyclist rides down a hill, along a flat road, then up a hill. Which speed–time graph is correct?
misconceptions.correct: Speed rises, stays roughly constant, then falls.
misconceptions.typical_wrong: A graph shaped like the hill and valley.
misconceptions.why: Visual features of the scene are matched to the graph's shape.

misconceptions.name: Slope–height confusion
misconceptions.description: Height of a graph is used where slope is needed.
misconceptions.example: Two distance–time graphs cross at t = 4. At t = 2, which object moves faster?
misconceptions.correct: The one with the steeper line.
misconceptions.typical_wrong: The one that is higher (has travelled farther) at t = 2.
misconceptions.why: Height is a more salient feature than slope.

misconceptions.name: Slope confused with visual steepness
misconceptions.description: The numerical slope is inferred from how steep a line looks after a change of axis scale.
misconceptions.example: The line y = x is drawn with 1 unit on the y-axis twice as long as 1 unit on the x-axis. It looks steeper than 45°. What is its slope?
misconceptions.why: Algebraic slope and geometric angle are treated as the same thing.

misconceptions.name: Function must have a formula or change
misconceptions.description: A constant relation is not accepted as a function.
misconceptions.example: Is y = 5 a function of x?
misconceptions.correct: Yes: every x gives exactly one y (namely 5).
misconceptions.typical_wrong: No, a function must change or contain x.
misconceptions.why: Concept image differs from the formal definition.

misconceptions.name: Every linear function is proportional
misconceptions.description: Doubling x is assumed to double y for any linear function.
misconceptions.example: For y = 2x + 3, if x is doubled, is y doubled?
misconceptions.correct: No: e.g. x = 1 gives y = 5, x = 2 gives y = 7.
misconceptions.typical_wrong: Yes, it is a straight line.
misconceptions.why: Linear and proportional relations are conflated.

misconceptions.name: Prototype-bound concept of triangle
misconceptions.description: Only shapes close to a prototype (symmetrical, base down) are accepted.
misconceptions.example: A scalene triangle is drawn tilted on one side. Is it a triangle?
misconceptions.correct: Yes: any closed shape with three straight sides is a triangle.
misconceptions.typical_wrong: No, it is not a proper triangle.
misconceptions.why: The concept image is tied to a familiar prototype figure.

misconceptions.name: A square is not a rectangle
misconceptions.description: Classes of shapes are treated as separate rather than nested.
misconceptions.example: Is every square also a rectangle?
misconceptions.correct: Yes: a square has all the properties of a rectangle.
misconceptions.why: Partitional classification based on appearance and prototypes.

misconceptions.name: Angle size read from arm length
misconceptions.description: The drawn length of the arms is confused with the amount of opening between them.
misconceptions.example: Angle A is 40° and has long arms. Angle B is 60° and has short arms. Which angle is larger?
misconceptions.typical_wrong: Angle A, because its arms are longer.
misconceptions.why: The opening is the least salient feature of the angle; the arms are what is seen.

misconceptions.name: Rectangle covering not seen as rows and columns
misconceptions.description: The number of unit squares is built by adding the sides or by counting single squares, not by multiplying rows by columns.
misconceptions.example: A rectangle is covered with 1 cm × 1 cm squares in 3 rows of 5 squares. How many squares are there?
misconceptions.why: The row-and-column structure of the array is not seen, so the two numbers are added.

misconceptions.name: Area units converted with the linear factor
misconceptions.description: The conversion factor between length units is applied unchanged to area units.
misconceptions.example: How many square centimetres are in one square metre?
misconceptions.why: 1 m = 100 cm is carried over to m² and cm².

misconceptions.name: Longer decimal is larger
misconceptions.description: The decimal with more digits is judged larger.
misconceptions.example: Which is larger: 0,45 or 0,6?
misconceptions.why: Digits after the comma are read as a whole number (45 > 6).

misconceptions.name: Shorter decimal is larger
misconceptions.description: The decimal with fewer digits is judged larger.
misconceptions.example: Which is larger: 0,4 or 0,45?
misconceptions.why: Hundredths are believed to be larger than tenths (as with 1/100 vs 1/10 reversed).

misconceptions.name: Whole-number bias in fraction addition
misconceptions.description: Numerators and denominators are added separately.
misconceptions.example: Calculate 1/8 + 1/8.
misconceptions.why: Numerator and denominator are treated as independent whole numbers.

misconceptions.name: Multiplication always makes bigger
misconceptions.description: The result of multiplying is expected to exceed both factors.
misconceptions.example: Is 0,5 × 8 greater or smaller than 8?
misconceptions.why: Whole-number experience: multiplying makes larger.

misconceptions.name: Division always makes smaller
misconceptions.description: The result of dividing is expected to be less than the dividend.
misconceptions.example: Calculate 8 ÷ 0,5.
misconceptions.why: Whole-number experience: dividing makes smaller (or halving is applied).

misconceptions.name: No number between 0,3 and 0,4
misconceptions.description: Rational numbers are treated as discrete, like whole numbers.
misconceptions.example: How many numbers lie between 0,3 and 0,4?
misconceptions.why: Natural-number successor thinking is applied to decimals.

misconceptions.name: Wrong base in reverse percentage
misconceptions.description: The given (new) amount is treated as the base value.
misconceptions.example: A can now holds 180 g, which is 20 % more than last year. How much did it hold last year?
misconceptions.why: The 20 % is taken from the new amount instead of the original amount.

misconceptions.name: Successive percentage changes
misconceptions.description: A rise and a fall of the same percentage are assumed to cancel.
misconceptions.example: A number of visitors rises by 10 % and then falls by 10 %. Compared with the start, the number has:
misconceptions.why: Percentages are treated as equal absolute amounts, ignoring the changing base.

misconceptions.name: Multi-digit number read as separate digits
misconceptions.description: A number such as 706 is handled as single digits placed side by side, so the value of a digit does not depend on its place.
misconceptions.example: In the number 706, what is the value of the digit 7?
misconceptions.why: The digit is read by its face value; tens, hundreds and ones are not treated as units.

misconceptions.name: Smaller digit subtracted from larger
misconceptions.description: When the top digit in a column is smaller, the smaller digit is subtracted from the larger one, so no regrouping takes place. Two related variants: the next digit is also reduced by one, or regrouping is done but the next digit is not reduced.
misconceptions.example: Calculate 453 − 127.
misconceptions.typical_wrong: 334 (3 − 7 taken as 7 − 3). Related wrong answers: 324 and 336.
misconceptions.why: Regrouping across a zero is avoided by reversing the subtraction in the column.

misconceptions.name: Smaller digit subtracted from larger; no regrouping
Smaller from larger, and the next digit is also reduced by one
Regrouping done in the column, but the next digit is not reduced
Wrong operation when the multiplier is below 1
misconceptions.description: Multiplication is seen only as repeated addition of equal groups, so a multiplier below 1 seems to call for division.
misconceptions.example: One metre of ribbon costs 4 €. Which calculation gives the price of 0,5 m?
misconceptions.why: A repeated-addition model needs a whole-number multiplier; with 0,5 the situation no longer fits it.

misconceptions.name: Larger denominator means larger fraction
misconceptions.description: Whole-number ordering is applied to the numerator and denominator separately.
misconceptions.example: Which is larger: 1/4 or 1/8?
misconceptions.why: The denominator 8 is larger than 4, so the fraction is read as larger.

misconceptions.name: Multiplying by 10 taken as adding a zero
misconceptions.description: A shortcut rule is applied to the written digits without place-value understanding, so it fails with decimals.
misconceptions.example: Calculate 3,5 × 10.
misconceptions.why: "Add a zero" is applied to the written digits; the digits are not seen as moving one place.

misconceptions.name: Recency (gambler's fallacy)
misconceptions.description: Past outcomes of a random process are assumed to influence the next.
misconceptions.example: A fair coin has landed heads 4 times in a row. What is the probability of heads on the next toss?
misconceptions.why: Belief that a random sequence must 'balance out' in the short run.

misconceptions.name: More black marbles means higher chance
misconceptions.description: The absolute count is used instead of the proportion.
misconceptions.example: Jar 1 has 6 black marbles out of 8. Jar 2 has 3 black marbles out of 4. Which jar gives the higher chance of drawing black?
misconceptions.typical_wrong: Jar 1, because it has more black marbles.
misconceptions.why: An intuitive rule: more of one quantity (black marbles) means more of another (chance).

misconceptions.name: Illusion of linearity: area
misconceptions.description: Doubling the side is assumed to double the area.
misconceptions.example: The side of a square is doubled. The area becomes:
misconceptions.why: A proportional (linear) model is applied where the relation is quadratic.

misconceptions.name: Illusion of linearity: volume
misconceptions.description: Doubling the edge is assumed to double the volume.
misconceptions.example: The edge of a cube is doubled. The volume becomes:
misconceptions.why: A proportional model is applied to a cubic relation.

misconceptions.name: Same perimeter means same area
misconceptions.description: Equal perimeters are assumed to imply equal areas ('same A, same B').
misconceptions.example: A 5 cm × 1 cm rectangle and a 3 cm × 3 cm square have the same perimeter. Do they have the same area?
misconceptions.why: An intuitive rule: if one quantity is equal, the other is equal too.

misconceptions.name: Larger perimeter means larger area
misconceptions.description: A rise in perimeter is assumed to raise the area ('more A, more B').
misconceptions.example: Shape P has a larger perimeter than shape Q. Must P also have a larger area?
misconceptions.typical_wrong: Yes, a longer boundary encloses more.
misconceptions.why: An intuitive rule: more of one quantity means more of another.
